system: You are a helpful assistant. Make sure your answer addresses every request in the message.
message:
I'm redoing our downstairs bathroom floor myself (first time, slightly terrified) and I've got a pile of questions.

The tile shop guy talked really fast so I didn't catch half of it. Could you explain what "lippage" means in tiling, in simple terms? And what's a sensible grout colour for a pale grey porcelain tile if I don't want it looking dirty after a month? My partner also wants to know whether we should do the floor before or after the new toilet goes in, just a quick answer with a reason.

The floor is 2.4 m by 1.8 m. The tiles I like are 30 cm × 60 cm and come in boxes of 8. Everyone online says to add 10% for cuts and breakages. How many boxes do I actually need to buy?

I also need a short, polite message to the neighbours saying there'll be some noise from cutting tiles on Saturday morning, since they've already put up with a skip on the drive for a fortnight. Finally, any three tips for a beginner laying their first floor would be very welcome. I've watched a lot of videos, but they all make it look far easier than it probably is.

Thank you, honestly.
response:
Good questions, and being a bit terrified before a first floor is a sensible place to start.

**What "lippage" means**
Lippage is when the edge of one tile sits higher than its neighbour, so you get a small step between them instead of a flat surface. It's a trip hazard, it catches dirt and mop heads, and it looks sloppy. It usually comes from an uneven subfloor or from pressing tiles in inconsistently. Larger tiles like yours (30 × 60) show it more, which is why a flat base matters.

**Grout colour**
Choose a mid-grey, one or two shades darker than your tile. White or very pale grout will stain and look grubby quickly, and black or charcoal shows every bit of limescale and dust against pale tile. A mid-grey hides everyday dirt and still looks deliberate. Seal it after it cures, or use a stain-resistant grout.

**Floor before or after the toilet?**
Tile first, then fit the new toilet. You get an uninterrupted floor with no awkward cuts around the base, and the toilet sits neatly on the finished surface. Just make sure the waste pipe or flange height suits the new tile thickness.

**How many boxes?**
- Floor area: 2.4 m × 1.8 m = 4.32 m²
- One tile: 0.3 m × 0.6 m = 0.18 m², so you need exactly 24 tiles
- Add 10%: 24 × 1.1 = 26.4, which rounds up to 27 tiles
- Boxes of 8: 27 ÷ 8 = 3.4, so you need **4 boxes** (32 tiles)

Three boxes (24 tiles) would leave you with nothing for cuts, so 4 is right. The 5 spare tiles are a useful cushion for a first-timer, and a couple kept for future repairs is worth having. Make sure all four boxes come from the same batch, because shades can vary slightly between batches.

**Message to the neighbours**
> Hi both, just a quick heads-up that I'll be cutting tiles for our bathroom floor on Saturday morning, so there'll be some noise for a while. I'll keep it to reasonable hours and finish as quickly as I can. Thank you so much for being so patient with the skip these past couple of weeks. It's really appreciated. Do let me know if there's a time that would suit you better!

**Three tips for a first floor**
1. **Dry-lay before you stick anything.** Lay the tiles out without adhesive, starting from the centre of the room, so you can see where the cuts fall. Avoid ending up with thin slivers at the walls or at the doorway.
2. **Get the subfloor flat and clean first.** Most lippage and wobbly tiles come from skipping this. Check with a long straight edge, fix any dips, and prime if the adhesive instructions call for it.
3. **Work in small sections and use spacers and a levelling system.** Mix only as much adhesive as you can use in the time it stays workable. Comb it in one direction, press each tile in with a slight twist, and check it's level with its neighbours as you go. Levelling clips are cheap and make a big difference with large tiles.

Good luck with it. Taking it slowly and dry-laying first will get you a long way.
